opus-5.5.text:
Early on, we didn't start with a fixed view of what the product should be. We started by sitting very close to the people building agents and watching what they actually tried to do with the web. That turned out to be far more instructive than any theory we had going in.

The first thing that jumped out was that the shape of the query was completely different. When a human searches, they type a few keywords, scan ten blue links, click one, and refine. An agent doesn't work that way. It often arrives with a rich, multi-part objective: "find companies that meet these five criteria, with evidence for each." Customers were taking those objectives and chopping them into keyword searches, because that's what existing search APIs expected. Then they'd fetch pages, scrape them, stuff them into context, and hope the model could sort it out. That workflow was brittle and expensive, and it told us the interface itself was wrong. Search for agents should accept the objective, not just keywords.

The second thing was what came back. Search results built for humans are optimized for a click: a title, a snippet, a ranking that assumes a person will judge relevance in a second. An agent doesn't click. It reads tokens. So what customers really needed were the most relevant, information-dense excerpts, compressed to fit a context window, rather than a list of links they then had to crawl. Watching people burn tokens on boilerplate, navigation menus, and irrelevant paragraphs made it obvious that ranking and extraction had to be designed around the model as the consumer.

Third, we saw a spectrum of latency and depth. Some workflows needed a fast answer inside an interactive loop. Others were happy to wait minutes, or longer, if it meant a thorough, well-sourced result, such as enriching a large dataset or doing deep research. Human search collapses all of that into "fast results." For agents, we realized you want a dial, where you can trade compute and time for quality, and pay accordingly.

And finally, verifiability mattered a lot more than we initially expected. When agents act on information, customers want to know where each fact came from and how confident the system is. So citations and calibrated confidence became first-class, not an afterthought.

So the honest answer is that the customer workflows designed the product. Every awkward workaround people were building on top of human-oriented search was a signal of what a web built for AI should natively provide. Our job was to take those workarounds seriously and build the infrastructure so they wouldn't be necessary.

r002.rationale: The response says the team watched what agent builders actually did and found that more instructive than theory, explicitly grounding product decisions in customer workflows rather than theoretical evaluations.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the early customers taught us more than any thesis we had going in. When we started Parallel, we had a conviction that the web was going to be read mostly by machines, not people, and that the infrastructure built for a human typing ten words into a box and clicking on a blue link was the wrong shape for that. But we didn't know what the right shape was. So we did something pretty unglamorous: we just went and sat with teams who were trying to get agents to do real work on top of the web, and we watched where they broke.

And a few patterns showed up almost immediately. The first was that agents don't ask one question. A human runs a search, scans the results, refines. An agent running a research task might issue dozens or hundreds of queries, and what it actually wants isn't ten links, it's the evidence. It wants the specific passage, the table, the number, with a source it can cite. So we stopped thinking about returning pages and started thinking about returning the right tokens, ranked for a model's context window rather than for a human eye.

The second thing was that the tasks were enormously varied in how much effort they deserved. One customer was doing lightweight enrichment, basically "find this company's website and headcount," at huge volume, where latency and cost mattered most. Another was doing deep due diligence where they were fine waiting minutes and paying more if the answer was actually right. The same API couldn't serve both unless we let the caller choose the depth. That's really where the idea of having explicit processor tiers came from. It wasn't a product idea in the abstract, it was watching two customers want opposite things from the same endpoint.

The third one, which I think is the most important, was verification. The failure mode nobody talks about enough is that an agent will happily synthesize a confident answer from a stale or wrong page. Customers didn't just want results, they wanted to know how much to trust each result. So we started building in things like per-field confidence and citations as first-class outputs, because that's what let them put the system into production without a human reviewing every row.

The meta-lesson was that you can't design search for agents by reasoning about it. You have to instrument real workflows, look at the queries agents actually generate, look at where they loop or hallucinate, and let that shape the product. We still work that way. Every new capability basically starts as a customer's broken workflow.

r001.rationale: The response says agents would read the web and describes teams using agents for web tasks, but it does not identify outsourced human work on web data as Parallel’s initial replacement target.

r002.rationale: It says the team sat with customer teams, observed where their agents broke, and let real workflows shape the product rather than relying on an abstract thesis.

astra-6.text:
We started with the workflows customers were trying to build. What information did an agent need, and what would it do with that information once it found it? That gives you a different way to think about search than starting with a query and a list of links.

For example, if an agent is researching a company, finding a relevant page is only an intermediate step. It still needs to extract the right facts, resolve conflicting information, and produce something grounded in sources. So the question becomes: how much of that work should the search system do, and what should it return so the agent can reliably take the next step?

Those early workflows were useful because they made the tradeoffs concrete. Sometimes speed matters most; sometimes you need to spend more time finding evidence. The way to judge the system is whether it helps the agent complete the task. That’s the lens we brought to what search for agents should look like.

sol-6.1.text:
We started with what customers were actually trying to accomplish. What information did the agent need, how was it going to use that information, and what would make the task successful? That gave us a much more useful starting point than taking a search interface designed for a person and putting an API around it.

For example, finding a relevant page isn’t necessarily the end of the job for an agent. It may need to extract a fact, compare it with another source, and use it in a larger workflow. So we looked at the whole loop: what the agent asked for, what came back, and whether that helped it take the next step.

The early workflows were a way to make those requirements concrete. They helped us think about search as a component that produces useful evidence for a task, rather than just a list of links.
